prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an interesting and timely problem: how to preserve the interpretability benefits of concept bottleneck models when they are deployed on top of foundation-model features under distribution shift. The central claim is that CBMs are not automatically robust simply because they operate through concepts, and that test-time adaptation should be applied at the concept layer and classifier layer, potentially with residual concepts added online. The proposed method, CONDA, combines three stages: concept-score alignment using source-domain Gaussian statistics in concept space, linear-probe adaptation using pseudo-labels, and a residual concept bottleneck branch to capture missing target-domain concepts. The empirical section evaluates several CBM construction methods across low-level, concept-level, and natural shifts.

Overall, I find the paper promising and potentially impactful. The problem is important, the framing is intuitive, and the empirical gains on several benchmarks are substantial, especially on Waterbirds and Metashift where unadapted CBMs degrade sharply. The paper also makes a useful conceptual point: interpretability via a bottleneck does not imply robustness under shift, and in fact the bottleneck can become a liability if the concept bank is incomplete or misaligned. That message alone is valuable for the community. At the same time, I have several concerns about the technical formulation, the strength of the evidence for some claims, and the extent to which the method’s gains should be attributed specifically to “concept adaptation” rather than to a fairly strong pseudo-labeled test-time fine-tuning procedure on a shallow classifier.

The main strength of the paper is the problem formulation and decomposition into failure modes. The distinction between non-robust concept extraction, non-robust concept-to-label mapping, and incomplete concept sets is a useful lens for thinking about CBMs under shift. Even if the formalism is somewhat idealized, it helps motivate why different adaptation mechanisms may be needed. I also appreciate that the method is source-free at adaptation time except for retained summary statistics, which is a realistic deployment setting. The use of multiple CBM construction methods is another positive aspect, since it suggests the approach is not tied to a single concept-bank pipeline.

The empirical results are encouraging. On Waterbirds and Metashift, CONDA often recovers a large fraction of the gap between unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable baselines, and sometimes reaches parity. The worst-group improvements are especially notable and relevant for spurious-correlation settings. The component analysis is also directionally sensible: concept-score alignment helps more on corruption-like shifts, while classifier adaptation and residual concepts matter more on semantic/contextual shifts. This is a coherent story and one of the stronger parts of the paper.

That said, the paper currently overstates some of its theoretical and empirical conclusions. My biggest concern is that the adaptation pipeline relies heavily on pseudo-labels produced by an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors from the same foundation model. This is a strong source of supervision. In effect, the method is allowed to borrow robustness from non-interpretable predictors at test time and distill it into the CBM. That is not inherently problematic, but it changes the interpretation of the contribution. The gains may reflect that the FM already solves the target task reasonably well under shift, and CONDA is mainly transferring those predictions into a concept-constrained shallow model. If so, the paper should be more explicit that the method is not improving robustness from concepts alone, but rather adapting the interpretable head using pseudo-supervision from stronger black-box predictors. This is especially important because the abstract and introduction sometimes suggest that the CBM itself is being made robust in a more intrinsic sense.

Relatedly, the comparison to non-interpretable baselines is not fully satisfying. The paper compares adapted CBMs to zero-shot and linear probing, but does not appear to compare against straightforward source-free adaptation of a shallow feature-based classifier using the exact same pseudo-labels and optimization budget. A very important baseline would be: take the FM features, adapt only a linear classifier on top using the same pseudo-labeling strategy and online batching, perhaps with or without a residual linear branch. Another baseline would be to adapt the full effective linear map W C directly without preserving the bottleneck factorization. Without such baselines, it is difficult to isolate whether the concept bottleneck structure is helping adaptation, or whether any low-capacity pseudo-labeled adaptation would achieve similar gains. Since Eq. (5) shows the final predictor is still linear in FM feature space, this question is central.

A second major concern is the novelty and necessity of the individual components. CSA is inspired by prior class-aware feature alignment methods, LPA is essentially pseudo-labeled linear-head adaptation with elastic-net regularization, and RCB resembles adding residual capacity to compensate for concept incompleteness. The combination is reasonable, but the paper should more carefully justify why the specific factorized adaptation through concepts is preferable to simpler alternatives. The current ablation narrative says different components matter under different shifts, but the evidence presented in the main paper is limited and somewhat mixed: in several cases, using only a subset of components outperforms the full method. This suggests the full pipeline may not be robustly beneficial and may require shift-type-dependent tuning. If the method is to be positioned as a general deployment framework, the paper should discuss how one would choose which components to activate without labeled target data.

The formal treatment of distribution shifts is also weaker than it first appears. The definitions of low-level and concept-level shift are framed in terms of equality or inequality of push-forward distributions under a chosen concept map and classifier. But these are not operationally testable definitions, and they depend on the very concept map whose robustness is under question. In particular, defining low-level shift as one that leaves the concept-score distribution unchanged seems circular when the first failure mode is precisely that the concept mapping may not be robust to such shifts. The paper partly acknowledges this by defining “non-robust concept bottleneck under low-level shift,” but then the taxonomy becomes more descriptive than formal. I do not think this invalidates the method, but the paper should tone down the formal claims and present the taxonomy as an intuitive decomposition rather than a rigorous characterization of shift types.

There are also some technical issues in the method section that need clarification. The Mahalanobis-based CSA assumes access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source-domain concept scores. This is a nontrivial retained artifact from training, and its storage and estimation quality may matter substantially, especially for large concept dimensions or many classes. For CIFAR100, covariance estimation in concept space could be unstable unless strong regularization or diagonal approximations are used, but the paper does not clearly explain how covariance matrices are regularized or inverted in practice. This is important because the CSA objective depends critically on these inverses. Similarly, the log ratio of intra- and inter-class Mahalanobis distances may be numerically unstable when distances are small or noisy. More implementation detail is needed.

The pseudo-labeling procedure also deserves more scrutiny. The paper chooses the class predicted with higher confidence between zero-shot and linear probing. This is simple, but it may introduce systematic bias toward whichever predictor is overconfident rather than more accurate. It would be useful to report pseudo-label accuracy, confidence calibration, and sensitivity to thresholding or filtering. Since the entire adaptation depends on pseudo-label quality, this is not a minor detail. In fact, one could imagine that on datasets where the FM is already robust, pseudo-labels are excellent and adaptation works well; where the FM is weaker, the method may fail. The paper hints at this in limitations/future work, but the main text should be more explicit.

The interpretability claims are interesting but currently under-supported. The paper argues that adapted concepts become “better aligned with the test data” and that residual concepts correspond to meaningful attributes such as feathers, wings, and beak. However, the evidence shown is anecdotal. Since the method modifies concept vectors continuously and adds randomly initialized residual concepts optimized for predictive performance, there is a real risk that interpretability degrades even if post hoc nearest-neighbor visualizations look plausible. More rigorous evaluation would help: concept purity/coherence metrics, human evaluation of concept labels, stability across runs, sparsity of concept usage, or comparison to known ground-truth attributes where available. In particular, if residual concepts are discovered solely from unlabeled target data and pseudo-labels, it is not obvious that they remain semantically disentangled rather than becoming arbitrary discriminative directions.

I also noticed some inconsistencies and possible overclaims in the presentation. The contribution list in the introduction includes a statement about “dominant languages” and “low-resource languages,” which appears unrelated to the rest of the paper and likely an editing artifact. This should be corrected. There are also a few equation/reference inconsistencies; for example, the text in Section 3.2 refers to Eq. (3) when it seems to mean the target-domain CBM equation later numbered as Eq. (5). Such issues are minor individually but reduce confidence in the polish of the submission.

The experimental section would benefit from stronger baselines and clearer reporting. First, as noted above, compare against feature-space TTA with the same pseudo-labels and online adaptation protocol. Second, compare against adapting only the effective linear map induced by the CBM, without concept constraints. Third, compare against a residual linear head in feature space rather than residual concepts, to test whether the residual branch’s benefit is specifically conceptual. Fourth, include a baseline that uses self-labeling from the CBM itself, to quantify how much of the gain comes from the FM pseudo-label teacher. Fifth, report adaptation hyperparameters and whether they are tuned per dataset or globally. If tuned per dataset or per shift type, that weakens the deployment realism.

The results table is interesting but also raises questions. On CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, some CBM variants actually worsen with CONDA, especially the Yeh et al. method. On Camelyon17, adaptation sometimes hurts the strongest unadapted CBM. These failures are important and should be analyzed rather than glossed over. Why does adaptation degrade performance for some concept banks? Is it due to pseudo-label noise, overfitting, or incompatibility between the concept construction method and the adaptation objectives? Understanding these cases would make the paper stronger and more credible.

Another concern is fairness of backbone selection. For CIFAR, the paper uses an adversarially fine-tuned robust CLIP variant, while for other datasets it uses standard CLIP or BioMedCLIP. This is reasonable from an application standpoint, but it complicates the narrative that the method is broadly effective independent of FM robustness. Since pseudo-label quality likely depends strongly on backbone robustness, the paper should disentangle the contribution of the FM from that of CONDA more carefully. The appendix may address this, but the main paper should summarize the dependence more explicitly.

I also think the paper should discuss the interpretability-performance tradeoff more honestly. Once the residual branch is added, the model effectively expands the concept bank with learned directions that may not correspond to pre-specified human concepts. If these residual concepts require automated captioning after the fact, the resulting system is arguably less interpretable than a standard CBM with fixed human-understandable concepts. This does not negate the contribution, but it changes the nature of the interpretability guarantee. The paper currently presents RCB as enhancing both interpretability and robustness; I think that claim needs qualification.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has merit. The problem is novel enough, the empirical story is compelling in several settings, and the idea of adapting concept bottlenecks rather than only black-box heads is worth exploring. My recommendation would depend on the conference bar and on whether the missing baselines and clarifications are available in the appendix or rebuttal. In its current form, I view the paper as borderline accept: strong motivation and promising results, but insufficiently convincing isolation of what is uniquely gained by concept-based adaptation.

To strengthen the paper, I would suggest the following concrete revisions. Add direct feature-space adaptation baselines under the same pseudo-labeling and optimization setup. Clarify covariance estimation, regularization, and numerical stability in CSA. Report pseudo-label accuracy and sensitivity analyses. Expand interpretability evaluation beyond qualitative examples. Analyze failure cases where CONDA hurts performance. Clarify whether hyperparameters are global or dataset-specific. Tone down the formalism around shift taxonomy and the claims about intrinsic robustness. Finally, fix the apparent editing artifact about languages and any equation/reference inconsistencies.

In summary, this is an interesting and potentially impactful paper on test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models on top of foundation models. Its main contribution is more empirical and conceptual than theoretical: it shows that CBMs can fail badly under shift and that targeted adaptation can often recover performance. The method is sensible and often effective, but the current evidence does not yet fully establish that the concept bottleneck structure itself is the key reason for the gains, nor that interpretability is preserved in a rigorous sense after adaptation. With stronger baselines and clearer analysis, this could become a strong paper.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. It argues that although FM-based CBMs can be accurate and interpretable on the source domain, they often degrade substantially under low-level, concept-level, and natural shifts. The proposed method, CONDA, adapts a deployed CBM using only unlabeled target data and no source samples through three stages: (1) concept-score alignment (CSA), which updates concept vectors to align target concept scores to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics using pseudo-labels and Mahalanobis distances; (2) linear probing adaptation (LPA), which updates the concept-to-label linear layer using pseudo-label cross-entropy with elastic-net regularization; and (3) a residual concept bottleneck (RCB), which adds new concept vectors and a residual linear head to compensate for incomplete concept sets. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show sizable gains over unadapted CBMs, often bringing performance closer to non-interpretable FM baselines. The paper also presents qualitative interpretability examples suggesting that adapted and residual concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: adapting interpretable CBMs built on foundation models under test-time distribution shift.
The proposed framework is modular and intuitively maps different adaptation components to different hypothesized failure modes: concept misalignment, classifier mismatch, and concept incompleteness.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple FM backbones, and multiple CBM construction methods, which strengthens the practical relevance of the study.
Results show substantial improvements over unadapted CBMs on several benchmarks, especially under concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift.
The paper includes some interpretability analysis of how concept importance changes after adaptation and how residual concepts may capture missing semantics.
The source-free adaptation setting is practically meaningful, and the use of unlabeled target data only is aligned with realistic deployment constraints.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing of shift types and completeness is largely definitional and does not yield formal guarantees, identifiable conditions, or testable consequences; several claims are therefore more heuristic than rigorous.

The method depends heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictions, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze failure cases when these pseudo-labels are poor or systematically biased.

CSA assumes access to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics of concept scores, which is a nontrivial form of source information and weakens the claimed source-free setting; the storage/privacy/feasibility implications are not fully discussed.

The Gaussian class-conditional assumption in concept space is strong and not empirically validated; no evidence is provided that Mahalanobis alignment is appropriate for the considered CBMs or datasets.

The residual branch undermines the strict interpretability promise of CBMs because newly learned concepts are optimized from unlabeled target data and only post-hoc annotated; their semantic faithfulness is not rigorously evaluated.

Some empirical outcomes are inconsistent with the broad claims: CONDA degrades performance in several settings (e.g., some CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 combinations, and zero-shot baselines can remain stronger than adapted CBMs), but these limitations are not deeply analyzed.

Comparisons are incomplete with respect to stronger generic test-time adaptation baselines applied directly to FM features or to the CBM classifier, making it hard to isolate the unique benefit of concept-aware adaptation.

The paper appears to contain at least one inconsistent claim in the introduction/contributions about language-related performance biases ('dominant languages' and 'low-resource languages'), which is unrelated to the presented vision experiments and suggests editing or content integrity issues.
methodological_flaws: The formalization of low-level shift in Eq. (2) assumes the concept-score distribution is unchanged under such transformations. This is not a property of the shift alone but of the pair (feature extractor, concept mapping). Since the paper later defines failure mode 1 precisely as violation of Eq. (2), the taxonomy is partly circular: a shift is called low-level if concept distributions are invariant, and failure is defined when they are not. This weakens the scientific logic of the categorization.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is problematic: it defines completeness by existence of a classifier g such that prediction distributions match across domains, but matching prediction distributions is not equivalent to preserving correct labels or sufficiency of concepts. A degenerate classifier with identical output distributions across domains could satisfy the definition without being accurate. Thus the definition does not capture semantic completeness in a scientifically meaningful way.

CSA minimizes log(D_intra/D_inter) using pseudo-labels and source Gaussian statistics, but there is no derivation showing that this objective approximates any principled divergence between source and target class-conditional concept distributions. The connection between the optimization objective and the stated alignment goal is heuristic rather than mathematically justified.

The Mahalanobis distance expression appears to contain a typographical/mathematical error in the text: D_mah is written with mismatched parentheses, suggesting insufficient care in the formal presentation. More importantly, invertibility/stability of class covariance matrices in high-dimensional concept spaces is not discussed; regularization of Sigma_y^{-1} is essential but omitted in the main method description.

The source-free claim is overstated because the method requires source-derived class means and covariances in concept space, as well as a source-trained linear probe for pseudo-labeling. This is source-data-free at adaptation time, but not source-information-free; the distinction matters scientifically and practically.

The empirical protocol may suffer from confirmation bias because pseudo-labels are generated using FM-based predictors that are also the performance targets the method aims to match. If pseudo-labels are strong, adaptation may simply distill the FM predictor into the CBM rather than genuinely discovering robust concept structure. The paper does not disentangle this effect.

Online adaptation on the same test stream used for evaluation can inflate performance relative to static deployment and is sensitive to batch order. The paper states batches are randomly split and processed sequentially, but robustness to ordering, stream composition, or repeated passes is not clearly established in the provided content.

Interpretability claims for residual concepts are weakly validated. Automatic captioning of learned residual vectors does not establish that these vectors correspond to coherent human concepts or causally meaningful factors; no human evaluation, intervention test, or concept fidelity metric is reported in the main text.

The empirical evidence does not consistently support the necessity of all three components: the paper itself notes that CSA alone or LPA alone can outperform the full method in some settings. This suggests the combined objective may be suboptimal or unstable, and the claimed mapping from failure modes to components is not fully validated.

There is an apparent content inconsistency in the listed contributions mentioning multilingual performance biases, which is unsupported by the experiments described. This raises concerns about manuscript quality control and whether parts of the text were copied from another context without proper integration.
